paragraphs: Posted by Lily. Nurse Jill visited the Explorers and gave each child a leaflet about hot days. She talked for twenty minutes, and she showed us a big poster. Teacher Kim read it with us, and now it is on the blog. Please read it, and show it to your family.

Our town is warm all year, so hot days are common. Young children get hot faster than adults. On a very hot day, you may feel tired, and you may have a headache. You may feel dizzy, and your heart may beat very fast. Your face may be red, and your body may feel very warm. These are the signs of too much heat. Tell an adult at once if you have one of these signs.

What should you do? First, go indoors or sit in the shade. Then sit down and drink a small glass of water. Put a cool wet cloth on your neck. Do not drink very cold water, because it may hurt your stomach. Open a window, or ask your teacher to turn on a fan. Rest for twenty minutes, and do not run or play. After that, check how you feel.

Some signs show danger. If a child cannot answer a question, call an adult immediately. If a child falls down or cannot stand, call an adult immediately too. Do not wait, because danger can grow fast. Speak calmly to the child, and do not give food or a drink. Stay with your friend until the nurse comes. The nurse will check the heart and the body of the child.

An accident can happen at any time, even on a day with no heat. For a small cut on a knee, wash it with clean water. Do not touch a cut with dirty hands. Then put a bandage on it, and tell the nurse. Wash your hands after you touch it. Always tell an adult about an accident, even a small one.

Sometimes a child feels ill for more than two days. Then Mom or Dad should make an appointment with a doctor. The doctor will say what the child needs. The nurse's room is open every school day, and you may visit it at any time. Remember to drink water, stay in the shade, and check on your friends. Nurse Jill ended her talk with a smile.
